answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1809–1849 · American poet, short-story writer & literary critic
answer.sourceLine: This is the ninth line of Poe’s poem “Annabel Lee,” completed in the months before his death and first printed just two days after it, in October 1849. The exact wording is unchanged across every one of the eleven documented manuscript and published versions of the poem.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: New-York Daily Tribune, October 9, 1849 (posthumous, unauthorized); first authorized printing in Sartain's Union Magazine, January 1850

source.excerpt: I was a child and she was a child, / In this kingdom by the sea, / But we loved with a love that was more than love— / I and my Annabel Lee— / With a love that the wingèd seraphs of heaven / Coveted her and me.
trail: Poe had completed “Annabel Lee” by May 1849, per a letter cited by the Edgar Allan Poe Society of Baltimore ↗, and gave manuscript copies to several acquaintances before his death that October.
It first reached print two days after Poe died, in Rufus Griswold's obituary notice in the New-York Daily Tribune ↗ (Oct 9, 1849).
The line appears with identical wording across all eleven surviving manuscript and print versions from 1849–1850, according to the Mabbott critical edition ↗.
The full poem, including this line, is preserved at Wikisource ↗ and reproduced by the Academy of American Poets ↗.
source.excerptNote: The popular standalone quotation drops the poem's opening word “But” and the closing em dash.

author.bio: Poe was a founding figure of American Gothic fiction and the modern detective story, best known for poems like The Raven and tales such as The Tell-Tale Heart. Annabel Lee was the last poem he completed, appearing in print only after his death in October 1849.

context.heading: The last poem Poe wrote
lead: “Annabel Lee” was among the very last things Edgar Allan Poe wrote, completed only months before he died in October 1849 under still-disputed circumstances. It tells of a childhood love so pure that envious angels “in Heaven” conspire to take the beloved away, leaving the narrator to keep loving her beyond death.

The poem is often read as an elegy connected to the women in Poe's life — most commonly his young wife Virginia Clemm Poe, who had died two years earlier — though Poe left no direct statement confirming a single inspiration.
